clue.text: Booker-winning book maker of The Playmaker

definitions.text: Booker-winning book maker of The Playmaker

parts.words: Booker-winning book maker of The Playmaker
parts.note: a 'book maker' sounds like a racecourse bookie, but here is an author who won the Booker Prize and also wrote the novel The Playmaker

explanation.surface: A literary quiz question asking for the prize-winning author of a novel about convicts staging a play.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Keneally won the Booker Prize in 1982 for Schindler's Ark and later wrote The Playmaker, about a play put on in an Australian penal colony.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Keneally, the Australian novelist, is the Booker winner who wrote The Playmaker.

clue.text: Fate intervened to some extent, when Barkis met Clara Peggoty

indicators.note: something that intervened partly sits between other things, so the letters are found inside the following words

explanation.surface: A moment from David Copperfield, where destiny takes a hand as Barkis meets Clara Peggotty.
explanation.walkthrough: Barkis and Clara Peggotty are a courting couple in Dickens's David Copperfield; the letters sit across 'BarKIS MET'.
explanation.definitionFit: Kismet is a Turkish-derived word for destiny or one's allotted lot.

clue.text: "Thou wouldst trip, like the s of Hogs-Norton, when the pigs play on the organ" (Scott)

definitions.text: "Thou wouldst trip, like the s of Hogs-Norton, when the pigs play on the organ" (Scott)

parts.words: "Thou wouldst trip, like the s of Hogs-Norton, when the pigs play on the organ" (Scott)
parts.note: a quotation from Walter Scott with one word left out before the plural s; the solver supplies the missing word, a term for simpletons

explanation.surface: A line of Walter Scott comparing someone's stumbling to the fools of a proverbial village.
explanation.walkthrough: The fill-in-the-blank quotation is from Scott's Kenilworth; 'Hogs-Norton' was a byword for a place of rustic fools, where pigs played the organ.
explanation.definitionFit: A noodle is an old word for a fool or simpleton, which is what Scott's villagers are.

clue.text: Following Emlyn Williams's repertory standby, will be Collins novel

definitions.meaning: Emlyn Williams's play Night Must Fall was a staple of repertory theatre; what comes after night falls is the time after sunset
Wilkie Collins published a collection of stories under this title in 1856

explanation.surface: A theatre note: after the reliable old Emlyn Williams thriller, the company will stage a Collins adaptation.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense needs the title of Emlyn Williams's thriller, Night Must Fall; following nightfall is when it is no longer light.
explanation.definitionFit: Following nightfall means once evening has turned to night, and Wilkie Collins used that phrase as the title of an 1856 book.

clue.text: Use spin later, perhaps, in waltz

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters of the phrase might be arranged another way

explanation.surface: Advice to a dancer to add a late twirl during a waltz.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges USE SPIN LATER. Les Patineurs, the Skaters' Waltz, is by Émile Waldteufel.
explanation.definitionFit: Les Patineurs (The Skaters) is the title of Waldteufel's famous waltz.

clue.text: Trap associated with Moth

definitions.meaning: Moth and ... are two of Titania's fairy attendants in A Midsummer Night's Dream

explanation.surface: An insect snare linked with a moth that blunders into it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moth' looks like the insect, but it is a fairy in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream; another fairy there shares its name with a spider's snare.
explanation.definitionFit: A spider's web catches flies, and in Shakespeare the fairy Cobweb serves Titania alongside Moth.

clue.text: Frank Yerby's was of holiness

parts.note: Frank Yerby wrote a novel titled 'An ... of Sanctity'; the clue swaps sanctity for holiness and asks for the missing noun

explanation.surface: A remark that a novelist's reputation, or perhaps aura, was a saintly one.
explanation.walkthrough: Frank Yerby's 1965 novel is An Odor of Sanctity; the phrase means a reputation for holiness.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase 'odour of sanctity' is a set idiom for a saintly smell or reputation, and Yerby used it as his title.

clue.text: Dumas-type duel with no second (possibly anagram)

indicators.note: with no tells us to take the given piece away from the longer word

parts.note: Dumas's musketeers fight with swords, so a duel of that kind is swordplay

explanation.surface: A Three Musketeers-style fight with no second present, with a sly hint about the puzzle itself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with no' removes S (second) from SWORDPLAY. 'Second' looks like a duelling attendant, but it is just its abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: An anagram is one kind of the verbal trickery that cryptic setters use, hence 'possibly'.

clue.text: Provenance of Kipling ballads

parts.note: Kipling's soldier poems were collected as Barrack-Room Ballads, so they come from soldiers' quarters

explanation.surface: A literary question about where Kipling's ballads came from.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's 1892 collection Barrack-Room Ballads gives voice to the British private soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: Kipling's ballads were named for the soldiers' living quarters they purported to come from.

clue.text: Sort of play that dare not speak its name

definitions.text: Sort of play that dare not speak its name

parts.words: Sort of play that dare not speak its name
parts.note: theatre superstition forbids naming Macbeth backstage, so actors refer to it by the nationality of its setting

explanation.surface: A play described like a forbidden love, echoing Lord Alfred Douglas's famous line.
explanation.walkthrough: Actors call Macbeth 'the Scottish play' to avoid bad luck; the wording echoes 'the love that dare not speak its name'.
explanation.definitionFit: The superstitious euphemism for Macbeth names it by its setting in Scotland.

clue.text: King's domain

parts.note: the king is the novelist Stephen King, and his domain is the genre he writes in

explanation.surface: A monarch's realm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'King' looks royal, but it is Stephen King, the American writer of frightening novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Stephen King is famed for terrifying fiction, so that genre is his territory.

clue.text: Acknowledged ghost?

parts.note: a ghostwriter normally goes uncredited; one whose help is credited on the title page is a co-author

explanation.surface: A spirit whose presence has been admitted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ghost' suggests a spectre, but it means a ghostwriter; once named, they become a credited partner.
explanation.definitionFit: A credited ghostwriter is a co-writer who worked jointly with the named author.

clue.text: English rule upset by Swiss mathematician

indicators.note: upset means the letters of the word rule are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: A Swiss mathematician overturning an English regulation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' looks like the rule being overturned in reversal, but it is an anagram signal; 'by' is a link. Euler was born in Basel.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonhard Euler was the great eighteenth-century mathematician born in Basel.

clue.text: Some questionable books

parts.note: certain scriptural books of doubtful authority are left out of many Bibles

explanation.surface: A remark about dubious titles on a shelf.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical writings outside the accepted canon are those of disputed authenticity.

clue.text: Car accessory from McMurtry

parts.note: a Cadillac is a make of American car
a jack, for lifting a car to change a wheel, is a standard car accessory

explanation.surface: A motoring accessory sold by someone named McMurtry.
explanation.walkthrough: Larry McMurtry, author of Lonesome Dove, wrote the 1982 novel Cadillac Jack.
explanation.definitionFit: Cadillac Jack is a novel written by Larry McMurtry, so it comes from him.

clue.text: Dramatist recalls poor Nellie on French horn

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means the second part is placed after the first

parts.note: cor is French for horn

indicators.note: poor suggests the name Nellie is in a bad way and so knocked out of shape

explanation.surface: A playwright remembering unfortunate Nellie playing the French horn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French horn' is the instrument on the surface but means the French word for horn, COR. 'poor' rearranges NELLIE to NEILLE; 'recalls' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Pierre Corneille was the seventeenth-century French tragic playwright of Le Cid.

clue.text: Cream perhaps no longer in favour of Australian novelist

parts.note: food or fashion that is off has gone bad or out of favour
Patrick White, Nobel laureate, was an Australian novelist

explanation.surface: Cream that has gone off, or perhaps an Australian writer fallen out of favour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cream' looks like the dairy product turning sour, but it is a pale colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Cream is an example of a pale shade just short of pure white.

clue.text: Writer taking part in carousal in Germany

indicators.note: taking part in says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: An author joining in a drinking session in Germany.
explanation.definitionFit: J. D. Salinger was the American author of The Catcher in the Rye.

clue.text: Outspoken English poet is sci-fi writer

parts.note: frank means candid or outspoken
George Herbert was a seventeenth-century English religious poet

explanation.surface: A blunt English poet turns out to be a science fiction writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Frank Herbert was the American author of the science fiction novel Dune.

clue.text: German car reportedly for Italian barrister

indicators.note: reportedly means we hear the car's name spoken rather than see it written

parts.note: Porsche is a German maker of sports cars

explanation.surface: A German car bought, by all accounts, for an Italian lawyer.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Merchant of Venice, Portia disguises herself as a young lawyer to defend Antonio.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Portia poses as a legal advocate in a Venetian court.

clue.text: "Some of a more ungainly make" (Fitzgerald)

parts.note: in FitzGerald's Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam the potter's shop holds clay pots, some more clumsily shaped than others

explanation.surface: A line from Edward FitzGerald describing awkwardly made things.
explanation.walkthrough: The quatrain describes the pots in a potter's house, which talk among themselves; some are lopsided.
explanation.definitionFit: FitzGerald's ungainly objects are clay pots, containers for liquid.

clue.text: Quietly spoken Nicholas Evans protagonist

definitions.meaning: one who speaks under the breath talks very softly
Nicholas Evans wrote The Horse ..., whose hero Tom Booker calms troubled horses

explanation.surface: A soft-voiced hero of a Nicholas Evans novel.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who murmurs speaks softly, and Evans's hero is a horse-calmer of that title.

clue.text: Song favoured by Gregory?

parts.note: Pope Gregory the Great gives his name to the unaccompanied chant of the medieval Church, also called by a simpler name

explanation.surface: A question about some man named Gregory's favourite tune.
explanation.walkthrough: Gregorian chant is also called plainsong; the answer is the first half of that word.
explanation.definitionFit: Plainchant, the simple unison church music linked to Pope Gregory, begins with this word.

clue.text: Record Oxford dictionary (new edition) in poetic form

parts.note: EP is an extended-play record

indicators.note: a new edition rearranges the material, so the letters of the dictionary's abbreviation are reordered

parts.note: OED is the Oxford English Dictionary

explanation.surface: A recording of a fresh edition of the Oxford dictionary, set in verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new edition' is printed in brackets but is the anagram signal working on the dictionary's abbreviation; an epode is the third section of a Pindaric ode.
explanation.definitionFit: An epode is a lyric verse form, or the part of a Greek ode following strophe and antistrophe.

clue.text: London colonel carries fashionable weight

parts.note: in means fashionable, as in 'the in thing'
a gram is a unit of weight

explanation.surface: A London army officer carrying a trendy load.
explanation.definitionFit: Ingram is a surname, here given to a colonel associated with London.

clue.text: High churchmen?

parts.note: rather than Anglo-Catholics, these are early Christian ascetics who lived on top of tall pillars

explanation.surface: A reference to Anglo-Catholic clergy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High' suggests the High Church, but it means physically high up; Simeon Stylites lived for decades atop a column.
explanation.definitionFit: Pillar saints such as Simeon spent their lives raised above the ground in devotion.

clue.text: Hesitate to carry on wandering

parts.note: er is the sound of someone hesitating
to carry on is to make a fuss or rant

explanation.surface: Advice to pause before continuing on a rambling journey.
explanation.definitionFit: A knight errant roams in search of adventure, so the word means roving.

clue.text: It showed the effect of gravity in Golding's work

definitions.text: It showed the effect of gravity in Golding's work

parts.words: It showed the effect of gravity in Golding's work
parts.note: a plunge under gravity alone, without a parachute open, is also the title of a William Golding novel

explanation.surface: A remark that a novel by William Golding demonstrated gravity.
explanation.walkthrough: Golding's 1959 novel Free Fall follows an artist's moral fall; gravity also means seriousness.
explanation.definitionFit: Unchecked descent under gravity gives the title of Golding's 1959 novel.
